title: Seat vs Venue in Arbitration Clauses: Why the Distinction Decides Which Court Can Intervene
seo_title: Arbitration Seat vs Venue: Which Court Controls?
meta_description: Why an arbitration clause's seat, not its venue, decides which country's courts can intervene, and what the 2024 Arif Azim ruling adds for such contracts.
intro: A foreign company negotiating a contract with an Indian counterparty, or an Indian company contracting with a foreign supplier, will often see an arbitration clause that names a city for hearings without using the word seat at all. That omission is not a drafting footnote; Indian courts treat the seat of arbitration, not the hearing venue, as the single fact that decides which country's courts can supervise, support or set aside the arbitration.

Getting this wrong in the drafting stage, or misreading it when a dispute actually arises, has real consequences: a party that assumes Indian courts can grant interim relief or hear a challenge to the award, when the clause actually fixes a foreign seat, can find its application dismissed as not maintainable, losing time it did not have.

sections.heading: What seat and venue actually mean
paragraphs: The seat of arbitration is the legal home of the arbitration, the jurisdiction whose arbitration law governs the proceeding and whose courts have supervisory authority over it, including the power to appoint an arbitrator where needed, grant interim relief, and hear a challenge to the resulting award. The venue, by contrast, is simply the physical place where hearings happen to be held for convenience, such as a city chosen because witnesses or counsel find it accessible, and it does not by itself carry any legal consequence.

A contract can validly name London as the venue for hearings while fixing the seat in India, or the reverse, and the two labels are frequently used loosely or interchangeably by parties drafting their own clauses without appreciating that only one of them determines which courts have authority. Where a clause uses only the word venue and never the word seat, Indian courts have had to work out, through a long line of decisions, when a stated venue should be read as the parties' intended seat.

sections.heading: The foundational rule from BALCO
paragraphs: The Supreme Court's Constitution Bench ruling in Bharat Aluminium Co. v. Kaiser Aluminium Technical Service, reported at (2012) 9 SCC 552, is the starting point for this entire area. The Court held that Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, which gives Indian courts their general supervisory powers over arbitration, applies only where the seat of arbitration is in India, adopting what is generally described as a seat-centric approach rather than one based on where the underlying contract or cause of action is most closely connected.

This matters because, before BALCO, Indian courts had in some cases asserted jurisdiction over foreign-seated arbitrations based on where the contract was substantially performed or where the parties were located, an approach BALCO rejected going forward for arbitration agreements entered into after the judgment. Once a foreign seat is fixed, Indian courts generally have no supervisory role over the arbitration itself, separate from the later question of enforcing a resulting foreign award in India.

sections.heading: BGS SGS Soma and reading a stated venue as the seat
paragraphs: In BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd, reported at (2020) 4 SCC 234, a three-judge bench addressed the common situation where a clause names a venue but is silent on the seat. The Court held that where an arbitration clause designates a particular place for the proceedings without any contrary indication that the place is meant to be merely a venue, naming that place carries with it the intention that it is actually the seat, because the parties would otherwise have said so expressly. The ruling treated the earlier decision in Hardy Exploration as inconsistent with the Constitution Bench's reasoning in BALCO and no longer good law on this point.

The practical effect is that a clause which simply fixes hearings in, for example, Singapore, without ever using the word seat, will usually be read as fixing Singapore as the seat as well, unless something else in the contract, such as a separate clause tying supervisory jurisdiction expressly to a different place, points the other way. Parties who actually intend the named city to be nothing more than a convenient hearing location, with the seat sitting elsewhere, need to say so clearly in the clause rather than leaving it to inference.

sections.heading: What the 2024 Arif Azim ruling adds for cross-border contracts
paragraphs: In Arif Azim Co. Ltd v. Micromax Informatics FZE, decided on 7 November 2024 and reported as 2024 INSC 850, the Supreme Court applied this seat-centric framework to a distributorship agreement between an Afghan company and a UAE-based entity that named Dubai as the venue, applied UAE governing law, and gave Dubai courts non-exclusive jurisdiction. The petitioner argued that because Dubai was only labelled a venue, and because the jurisdiction clause was non-exclusive rather than exclusive, Indian courts could still entertain a petition to appoint an arbitrator.

The Court held that the combination of the stated venue, the choice of UAE governing law, and the non-exclusive jurisdiction clause pointed together to Dubai being the intended seat, and dismissed the petition for appointment of an arbitrator under Section 11(6) of the Act as not maintainable before an Indian court. The ruling is a reminder that a non-exclusive jurisdiction clause pointing to a foreign court does not, on its own, preserve a path into Indian courts once the surrounding terms of the contract indicate a foreign seat; the assessment looks at the clause as a whole rather than at any single word in isolation.

sections.heading: Why this matters when drafting a clause for a cross-border contract
paragraphs: A foreign company contracting with an Indian counterparty should decide, consciously, whether it wants Indian courts to have any supervisory role at all, and draft the clause to say so in terms that use the word seat and, separately, the word venue if the two are meant to differ. Where the seat is fixed outside India, limited interim relief may still be available from an Indian court under the proviso to Section 2(2) of the Act unless the parties have expressly excluded it, which is a separate question from the general supervisory jurisdiction discussed above and is worth addressing explicitly in the clause rather than leaving to a later dispute.

An existing contract that only states a venue, with no seat clause and no clear indication either way, should not be assumed to default in any particular direction; it will fall to be read under the BGS SGS Soma approach, against the specific wording the parties actually used, including the governing law clause and any jurisdiction clause, as happened in Arif Azim. A party unsure whether its current contracts carry this risk is better served reviewing the dispute resolution clause now, while amending it is still a negotiation rather than a contested point in a live dispute.

faqs.q: What is the difference between seat and venue in an arbitration clause?
faqs.a: The seat is the jurisdiction whose courts have supervisory authority over the arbitration, including appointing arbitrators, granting interim relief and hearing a challenge to the award. The venue is simply the physical location chosen for hearings and carries no legal consequence by itself.

faqs.q: If a clause only names a venue and never says seat, which one applies?
faqs.a: Under the Supreme Court's ruling in BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd, a named venue is generally read as the intended seat unless the contract clearly indicates otherwise. Parties who want the named city to be only a hearing location, with the seat elsewhere, need to say so expressly.

faqs.q: Can Indian courts intervene in an arbitration seated outside India?
faqs.a: Generally no, for the general supervisory powers under Part I of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, following the Supreme Court's ruling in the BALCO case. Limited interim relief may still be available under the proviso to Section 2(2) unless the parties have expressly excluded it.

faqs.q: Does a non-exclusive foreign jurisdiction clause let a party still approach Indian courts?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. In Arif Azim Co. Ltd v. Micromax Informatics FZE, the Supreme Court held that a non-exclusive jurisdiction clause pointing to a foreign court, read together with the stated venue and governing law, still supported treating the foreign location as the seat, and dismissed the Indian court petition as not maintainable.

faqs.q: How should a cross-border contract be drafted to avoid this dispute?
faqs.a: Use the words seat and venue separately and expressly in the arbitration clause rather than naming only a city for hearings. State clearly which country's courts are meant to have supervisory authority, and address separately whether Indian interim relief under Section 2(2) is intended to remain available.

verification_notes: AUDIENCE: foreign company negotiating or disputing a cross-border contract with an Indian party. TARGET QUERY: 'seat vs venue arbitration India' / 'does naming a venue make it the seat' / 'can Indian courts intervene in foreign seated arbitration'. DEMAND EVIDENCE: none seen from an analytics tool; inferred from the continuing volume of law-firm commentary on the Arif Azim ruling published through late 2024 and into 2025, and from the seat-versus-venue question recurring as a distinct topic in SCC Online Blog commentary as late as May 2024, both indicating sustained practitioner interest rather than a one-off news cycle. That BALCO, (2012) 9 SCC 552, held Part I of the Act applies only where the seat is in India, prospectively from the judgment date, is confirmed from two independent sources (a Kluwer Arbitration Blog post and a Clifford Chance client briefing, both published at the time of the 2012 judgment). That BGS SGS Soma JV v. NHPC Ltd, (2020) 4 SCC 234, held a stated venue is generally read as the seat absent a contrary indication, and that it declared Hardy Exploration inconsistent with BALCO, is confirmed from two independent sources (the O.P. Jindal Global University ADR mapping project's case note and a LiveLaw report on the subsequent Arif Azim ruling that recaps the BGS SGS Soma holding). That Arif Azim Co. Ltd v. Micromax Informatics FZE, 2024 INSC 850, was decided on 7 November 2024, concerned a Dubai venue, UAE governing law and a non-exclusive jurisdiction clause, and resulted in dismissal of a Section 11(6) petition as not maintainable, is confirmed from at least three independent sources (LiveLaw, Casemine's case commentary and a Bar and Bench report), which agree on the date, citation and outcome; some secondary commentary differed on exactly how the judgment characterised the non-exclusive jurisdiction clause's effect, so that point is stated narrowly as what the Court held about the specific clause before it rather than as a sweeping rule about all non-exclusive clauses. The availability of interim relief under the Section 2(2) proviso for a foreign-seated arbitration unless expressly excluded is stated as the general statutory position under the 1996 Act as amended in 2015, rather than tied to a specific case verified in this research session.
